distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for systemic cryoglobulin-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. HCV, HBV, lymphoproliferative disease, autoimmune disease, infection, temperature exposure, organ dominance, and severity are represented as risk/context axes, treatment modifiers, or future related leaves rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: IgA vasculitis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, SLE flare, PAN, infectious endocarditis, DIC, thrombotic microangiopathy, lymphoma fever, and isolated monoclonal gammopathy without vasculitis remain competing manifolds or context.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: B-cell or plasma-cell driven production of cryoglobulins, most often mixed type II or III immune complexes and less often type I monoclonal immunoglobulin. The driver may be chronic viral antigen, autoimmune B-cell activation, or a lymphoproliferative clone, but those contexts are modifiers rather than part of the disease name.
Mixed cryoglobulins commonly contain IgM rheumatoid-factor activity binding polyclonal IgG, creating circulating immune complexes that deposit in small vessels and glomeruli.

Cryoglobulins precipitate at lower temperatures and in slow-flow vascular beds, producing luminal aggregates, hyaline thrombi, acral ischemia, livedo, ulcers, necrosis, and type I hyperviscosity phenotypes.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Classical complement activation and C4 consumption
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Immune complexes activate the classical complement pathway, typically producing disproportionately low C4 with variably low C3; this biochemical pattern is a central disease activity signal.
Immune-complex deposition in dermal post-capillary venules recruits neutrophils and causes leukocytoclasia, palpable purpura, petechiae, and recurrent dependent lower-extremity rash.

Glomerular immune-complex and cryoglobulin deposits cause endocapillary hypercellularity, double contours, intracapillary pseudothrombi, proteinuria, hematuria, nephrotic syndrome, and kidney function loss.
Small-vessel vasculitis and occlusion of vasa nervorum produce painful sensory neuropathy, weakness, mononeuritis multiplex, and incomplete neurologic recovery after delayed control.

Severe CryoVas can involve bowel, lung, CNS, or other organs through immune-complex vasculitis and microvascular occlusion, causing intestinal ischemia, pulmonary hemorrhage, cranial neuropathies, or multiorgan failure.
Active vascular inflammation and underlying immune drivers produce fever, fatigue, weight loss, elevated CRP/ESR, anemia of inflammation, and low albumin.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Detectable serum cryoglobulins are the direct laboratory expression of cryoglobulin production.
Higher cryoglobulin burden raises cryocrit, although sample handling affects measured values.
Monoclonal B-cell or plasma-cell clones may produce type I cryoglobulin patterns.
Mixed cryoglobulinemia often shows monoclonal IgM RF with polyclonal IgG.
Cryoglobulin-producing B-cell activity creates the RF-containing immune complexes that drive most mixed CryoVas.
RF positivity is common in mixed cryoglobulinemia and tracks humoral activity.
High RF titers reflect abundant IgM RF immune-complex activity.
Immune complexes consume classical complement, especially C4.
Disproportionately low C4 is a signature laboratory abnormality in CryoVas.
C3 may fall in severe immune-complex activation, though less consistently than C4.
Deposited immune complexes recruit neutrophils in dermal small vessels.
Precipitated cryoglobulins and hyaline thrombi intensify cutaneous vessel injury.
Palpable purpura is the classic cutaneous manifestation of dermal small-vessel vasculitis.
Purpuric and petechial rash may occur even when lesions are not described as palpable.
Reticular vascular flow disturbance and occlusion can produce livedo.
Severe cutaneous ischemia causes ulcers and necrosis.
Acral microvascular occlusion produces limb or digital ischemia.
Uncontrolled acral ischemia can progress to digital or limb gangrene.
Persistent cryoglobulin immune complexes deposit in glomeruli and cause MPGN.
Glomerular capillary wall injury increases protein leak.
Protein/creatinine ratio quantifies glomerular proteinuria.
Cryoglobulinemic MPGN may produce non-nephrotic or nephrotic-range daily proteinuria.
Active glomerulonephritis produces microscopic hematuria.
RBC casts and granular casts indicate active glomerular injury.
Severe or progressive cryoglobulinemic GN reduces GFR.
Nephrotic proteinuria and inflammation lower albumin.
Untreated MPGN can progress to severe kidney impairment or dialysis need.
Vasa nervorum injury causes sensory and motor neuropathy.
Patchy ischemic nerve injury can appear as mononeuritis multiplex.
Sensory loss and neuralgia are common neuropathy expressions.
Delayed control of vasculitic neuropathy can leave persistent weakness or neuralgia.
Bowel vasculitis or ischemia may present with abdominal pain.
Severe visceral vasculitis can cause intestinal ischemia and shock.
Pulmonary capillaritis or microvascular injury can cause alveolar hemorrhage in severe CryoVas.
CNS or cranial nerve ischemic vasculitis is uncommon but reported in severe disease.
Systemic inflammatory activity may cause fever.
CRP rises with active inflammation but may also reflect infection or tissue ischemia.
ESR commonly rises with immune-complex inflammation and hypergammaglobulinemia.
Chronic inflammation and kidney disease may lower hemoglobin.
Fatigue is a frequent systemic symptom.
Arthralgia is part of the classic CryoVas clinical triad with purpura and weakness.
Progressive acral ischemia creates risk of irreversible gangrene and amputation.
Extensive necrosis, hyperviscosity, and multiorgan ischemia increase acute mortality.
Severe renal involvement and dialysis need worsen prognosis.
Bowel ischemia, pulmonary hemorrhage, CNS involvement, and multiorgan failure are major acute mortality drivers.

axes.shape_free_text: Serum cryoglobulin detection when sample is collected and processed warm; false negatives occur with poor handling.
Measured cryoglobulin precipitate volume; severe manifestations can occur with modest cryocrit, especially type II disease.
Classically low and often disproportionately lower than C3 in mixed CryoVas.

Aggregate mortality hazard from severe renal failure, intestinal ischemia, pulmonary hemorrhage, extensive limb necrosis, infection during immunosuppression, and active underlying hematologic disease.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Higher circulating cryoglobulin burden increases risk of acral precipitation and ischemic lesions.
RF immune-complex activity consumes C4 in mixed CryoVas.
Both rise with falling GFR, modified by dialysis and prerenal physiology.
More intense cutaneous vasculitis increases ulcer and necrosis risk, but ischemic occlusion can dominate independently.
Established acral ischemia is the immediate precursor to gangrene and amputation.
Heavy proteinuria indicates active glomerular injury and predicts kidney outcome.
Rising creatinine during active GN increases kidney failure risk.
Severe or persistent neuropathy increases risk of residual disability.
Abdominal pain in severe CryoVas can be a clinical expression of bowel vasculitis or ischemia.
Intestinal ischemia and perforation can cause shock and death.
Pulmonary hemorrhage increases acute mortality through hypoxemia and respiratory failure.
High-dose steroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, dialysis, and active tissue necrosis increase fatal infection risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removing chronic HCV antigen reduces the driver of many mixed CryoVas cases.
Wrong, interrupted, or unavailable antiviral coverage will not reduce viral antigenic drive.

treatments.context_specific_role: Causal antiviral therapy for HCV-associated CryoVas; organ-threatening disease often also needs rapid immunomodulation while viral suppression emerges.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: B-cell clonal disease makes CD20 depletion more directly causal for cryoglobulin production.
HBV reactivation risk, severe hypogammaglobulinemia, or uncontrolled infection requires mitigation and may delay dosing.

side_effects.interpretation: B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinemia increase infection risk.
HBV screening and prophylaxis are required when relevant.

treatments.context_specific_role: Targets pathogenic B-cell activity in mixed CryoVas, lymphoproliferative-associated CryoVas, and refractory disease after antiviral control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe organ-threatening vasculitis needs immediate anti-inflammatory suppression.
Infection can mimic or coexist with CryoVas and is worsened by high-dose steroids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid bridge for moderate to severe vasculitic inflammation while antiviral, rituximab, plasma exchange, or clone-directed therapy changes the driver.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe ischemia or hyperviscosity benefits from rapid removal of circulating cryoglobulins.
No access, unstable hemodynamics, or inability to keep circuit and replacement fluid warm limits treatment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Fast temporary removal for life- or organ-threatening cryoglobulin burden such as rapidly progressive GN, pulmonary hemorrhage, intestinal ischemia, hyperviscosity, or severe acral necrosis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dose adjustment and infection risk constrain use in severe renal disease or dialysis.

side_effects.interpretation: Cytotoxic immunosuppression increases bacterial and opportunistic infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Used for selected severe systemic CryoVas when organ-threatening vasculitis is not controlled by antiviral, rituximab, plasma exchange, and steroids alone.
Adjunct or maintenance strategy when slower steroid-sparing control is needed after acute driver-directed therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: When a marginal-zone, lymphoplasmacytic, myeloma, or other clonal disorder is the driver, clone-directed therapy changes the source term for cryoglobulins.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treats the underlying hematologic source when CryoVas is driven by monoclonal B-cell or plasma-cell disease.
Reduces HBV reactivation hazard when rituximab or high-grade immunosuppression is used in patients with current or prior HBV markers.
Supports kidney outcome by reducing proteinuria and blood pressure load; it does not remove cryoglobulin immune complexes.
Local management for necrotic or infected tissue after systemic vascular control is addressed.

present.treatment_effect_modulation: makes hcv_direct_acting_antiviral_therapy causal for the upstream antigenic driver

sustained_virologic_response_with_persis.trajectory_modulation: cryoglobulin production may persist despite negative serum HCV RNA when B-cell clones remain active

present.treatment_effect_modulation: strengthens rituximab or clone-directed therapy and may weaken antiviral-only strategies

present.trajectory_modulation: amplifies cold precipitation, livedo, acral ischemia, ulcers, and gangrene without necessarily increasing CRP
raises renal laboratory base measure and increases treatment toxicity without implying active cryoglobulinemic GN by itself

older_than_65.trajectory_modulation: higher frequency of clonal B-cell disease and higher infection mortality during immunosuppression

present.trajectory_modulation: can trigger flare or mimic inflammatory activity; also increases steroid and rituximab risk
present.treatment_effect_modulation: weakens high-dose immunosuppression until infection is treated or excluded

present.trajectory_modulation: increases serious infection hazard and may require immunoglobulin replacement or prophylaxis
allows irreversible gangrene, neurologic disability, chronic kidney damage, or visceral ischemia before immune markers improve

supportive_care: Keep blood samples for cryoglobulin testing warm until serum separation; a negative cryoglobulin result with strong clinical suspicion should be interpreted cautiously.
Avoid cold exposure and keep affected limbs warm during active ischemic disease.
Assess hepatitis C, hepatitis B, HIV, autoimmune disease, and B-cell or plasma-cell clonal disease because treatment effects depend on the upstream driver.
Quantify renal involvement with urinalysis, urine protein/creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein, serum creatinine, albumin, complements, and kidney biopsy when safe.
Monitor skin necrosis, digital ischemia, neuropathy, abdominal pain, hemoptysis, and neurologic deficits as organ-threatening features rather than cosmetic rash.
Provide PJP prophylaxis, HBV prophylaxis when indicated, vaccination review, and infection surveillance when using rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or prolonged high-dose steroids.
Use renal-dose adjustment and dialysis coordination for antivirals, immunosuppressants, anticoagulation decisions, and plasma exchange timing.
Coordinate wound care, vascular surgery, pain control, rehabilitation, and debridement or amputation decisions when tissue loss is irreversible.
Treat hypertension, edema, and nephrotic complications with sodium restriction, diuretics when appropriate, RAAS blockade when tolerated, and thrombosis risk review.
Follow cryocrit, complement C4, RF, renal labs, skin and neurologic findings longitudinally because marker improvement can lag behind irreversible organ injury.
